oil.summary: Crude cratered for a second consecutive session as the US-Iran ceasefire deal and Hormuz reopening continued to unwind the geopolitical risk premium built up during the conflict. WTI shed 3.98% to $73.56/bbl and Brent fell 2.69% to $77.70/bbl, extending month-to-date losses beyond 25%. RBOB led the product complex lower, off 4.15%. The deal allows immediate Iranian oil sales, swamping the supply outlook. Options markets now price a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting, signalling producer pain. Offsetting factors remain: Trump flagged reimposition of Russian crude sanctions 'soon', India is on track for record Russian crude imports in June amid US waivers, and Saudi Arabia is still absorbing Russian fuel oil to offset domestic supply disrupted by the conflict. China, sitting on full storage, shows no urgency to resume imports.
drivers: US-Iran ceasefire and Hormuz reopening removes supply-disruption premium; Iranian barrels cleared for immediate sale
OPEC cut probability surges to 77% on options markets as prices collapse 25%+ in a month
Competing cross-currents: imminent reimposition of Russian sanctions threatens to tighten supply, while China's full inventories dampen near-term demand recovery

gas.summary: Natural gas prices diverged sharply by region. Henry Hub gained 2.78% to $3.323/MMBtu, extending a solid one-month rally of 10.62%, while European TTF surged 3.82% to €42.07/MWh on a confluence of acute risks. A major explosion and fire at Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG facility injured over 50 people and left 18 unaccounted for, threatening a key global LNG supply node at a precarious moment. Simultaneously, a European heatwave is lifting near-term power demand, and residual Hormuz uncertainty continues to cloud regional supply routes. On the structural side, China is developing a second terminal for sanctioned Russian LNG as its gas imports surge, reshaping long-term trade flows. Saudi Arabia's turn to Russian fuel oil for power generation underscores how the Iran-war supply shock continues to reverberate through fossil fuel markets.
drivers: Explosion at Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG facility raises immediate supply-disruption fears for global LNG flows
European heatwave boosting short-term power and gas demand, pushing TTF up nearly 4% on the day
China building second terminal for Russian LNG as imports surge, reshaping structural demand patterns away from traditional suppliers

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs firmed 1.12% to $76.995/EUA, notching a one-month gain of 8.63%, supported by tightening power-sector fundamentals. A European heatwave is driving near-term demand, while the Qatar LNG blast and residual Hormuz risk keep gas prices elevated, incentivising heavier carbon-intensive dispatch and supporting allowance prices. Saudi Arabia's pivot to Russian fuel oil for domestic power generation highlights how broadly the Iran conflict disrupted fossil-fuel power supply chains. On structural themes, major corporates publicly urged governments to accelerate electrification to reduce exposure to volatile fuel markets, while Chinese grid operators pushed back on plans to channel more renewables into AI data-centre loads, citing peak-demand reliability risks. Russia's fuel rationing in Crimea following Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure adds a further note of tightness to European energy balances.
drivers: European heatwave lifting power demand and gas burn, supporting EUA prices alongside elevated TTF
Qatar LNG explosion and lingering Hormuz uncertainty sustain fossil-fuel supply risk premium in carbon markets
Big business electrification push versus Chinese grid operator resistance to renewables-for-AI plans highlight divergent structural pathways for power-sector carbon demand
